questions.problem:
Which of the following vector spaces has a dimension of $6?$

I. ${R}_{5}[t]$, the vector space of all polynomials in the variable $t$ of degree at most $5$

II. ${R}^{5}$

III. ${\text{M}}_{6}(R),$ the vector space of all $6\times 6$ matrices over $R$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's examine each of the vector spaces in turn.

I. Recall that $\text{dim}({R}_{n}[t])=n+1.$ Therefore, 

  $$
  \text{dim}({R}_{5}[t])=5+1=6.\,✓
  $$

II. Recall that $\text{dim}({R}^{n})=n.$ Therefore, 

  $$
  \text{dim}({R}^{5})=5\ne 6.\,\times 
  $$

III. Recall that $\text{dim}({\text{M}}_{n}(R))={n}^{2}.$ Therefore, 

  $$
  \text{dim}({\text{M}}_{6}(R))={6}^{2}=36\ne 6.\,\times 
  $$

Hence, the correct answer is "I only."

questions.problem:
Which of the following vector spaces has a dimension of $16?$

I. ${R}_{15}[t]$, the vector space of all polynomials in the variable $t$ of degree at most $15$

II. ${\text{M}}_{4}(R)$, the vector space of all $4\times 4$ matrices over $R$

III. ${R}^{15}$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's examine each of the vector spaces in turn.

I. Recall that $\text{dim}({R}_{n}[t])=n+1.$ Therefore, 

  $$
  \text{dim}({R}_{15}[t])=15+1=16.\,✓
  $$

II. Recall that $\text{dim}({\text{M}}_{n}(\text{R}))={n}^{2}.$ Therefore, 

  $$
  \text{dim}({\text{M}}_{4}(R))={4}^{2}=16.\,✓
  $$

III. Recall that $\text{dim}({R}^{n})=n.$ Therefore, 

  $$
  \text{dim}({R}^{15})=15\ne 16.\,\times 
  $$

Hence, the correct answer is "I and II only."

questions.problem: What is the dimension of ${\text{M}}_{9}(R),$ the vector space of all $9\times 9$ matrices over $R?$
questions.worked_solution:
The standard basis of ${\text{M}}_{n}(R)$ contains a total of ${n}^{2}$ matrices, each with one nonzero entry that is equal to $1.$ 

For example, the standard basis of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$ contains ${2}^{2}=4$ elements, and is given by

$$
\{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}],\,[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\}.
$$

Therefore, for ${\text{M}}_{9}(R),$ we have

$$
\text{dim}({\text{M}}_{9}(R))={9}^{2}=81.
$$

In general, 

$$
\text{dim}({\text{M}}_{n}(R))={n}^{2}.
$$

questions.problem:
Which of the following vector spaces are finite-dimensional?

I. ${R}^{750}$

II. ${R}^{\infty },$ the vector space of infinite real sequences

III. ${\text{M}}_{50}(R),$ the vector space of all $50\times 50$ matrices over $R$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's examine our vector spaces.

- ${R}^{\infty }$ is *not* finite-dimensional. To understand why, we first note that the following set of sequences is linearly independent:

$$
\{{e}_{1},\,{e}_{2},\,…,{e}_{n}\},\,n\in N
$$

where, for each $j\in \{1,2,…,n\},$

$$
{e}_{j}=(0,…,0,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,{1,}_{{↑}_{{j}^{\text{th}}\text{ position}}}\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,0,…).
$$

Indeed, we have that 

$$
{\sum }_{i=0}^{n}{x}_{i}{e}_{i}=0
$$

if and only if ${x}_{i}=0$ for all $i=0,1,2,…,n.$ Therefore,  for any  $n\in N,$  there exists a linearly independent subset of ${R}^{\infty }$ of size $n,$ which imples that  ${R}^{\infty }$ cannot have finite dimension.

- ${R}^{750}$ and ${\text{M}}_{50}(R)$ are finite-dimensional. Indeed, 

$$
\text{dim}({R}^{750})=750,
$$

and

$$
\text{dim}({\text{M}}_{50}(R))={50}^{2}=2\,500
$$

 
are both finite numbers.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

questions.problem:
Which of the following vector spaces are finite-dimensional?

I. ${R}_{1000}[t],$ the vector space of all polynomials in the variable $t$ of degree at most $1\,000$

II. ${\text{M}}_{200\times 500}(R),$ the vector space of all $200\times 500$ matrices over $R$

III. $C,$ as a vector space over $R$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's examine our vector spaces.

- ${R}_{1000}[t]$ and ${\text{M}}_{200\times 500}(R)$ are finite-dimensional. Indeed, 

$$
\text{dim}({R}_{1000}[t])=1\,000+1=1\,001,
$$

and

$$
\text{dim}({\text{M}}_{200\times 500}(R))=200\cdot 500=100\,000
$$

 
are both finite numbers.

- $C$ is also finite-dimensional. To understand why, we first note that the following set of complex numbers is linearly independent:

$$
\{1,i\}
$$

Indeed, we have that 

$$
a\cdot 1+b\cdot i=0
$$

if and only if $a=0$ and $b=0.$ Since our vector space is also spanned by this linearly independent subset, we have that $\text{dim}(C)=2.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."
